newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - German Gehe clinches Lloyds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German Gehe clinches Lloyds.

text.p: German drug wholesaler and manufacturer Gehe AG clinched a tense, year-long fight for control of British retail chain Lloyds Chemists Plc on Monday after outgunning its rival Unichem Plc.

In the end the superior financial firepower of Stuttgart-based Gehe, which upped its cash bid for Lloyds on Friday to 525 pence per share from 500 pence, valuing LLoyds at 684 million pounds ($1.15 billion), proved too much for Unichem.

The British company effectively admitted defeat on Monday by refusing to raise its largely share-based bid, hoping vainly that the promise of "potential rewards" from the combination of Lloyds with its own retail chain Moss Chemists would be strong enough to sway Lloyds' shareholders.

But within 90 minutes of Unichem's statement Gehe said that it had already passed the magical 50 percent threshold for acceptances, and Lloyds' board said it would recommend the German offer to those shareholders still holding out.

Unichem, which has around 30 percent of Britain's drug wholesale market, found its attempt to make itself a major player in the retail sector fatally undermined by the scepticism of its own shareholders. As concern grew about the earnings dilution of a Lloyds' acquisition, so the value of its own bid sank in line with its share price.

Ironically, relief at the failure of the bid sparked a revaluation of Unichem on Monday, pushing its share price up 12-1/2 pence to 267 pence in early afternoon trading and putting the value of its own offer for Lloyds within spitting distance of Gehe's winning bid.

Gehe's victory follows an exhausting year-long tussle between the two companies which began with an agreed 493 million pound offer from Unichem on January 18, 1996. Gehe quickly responded with a 584 million pound bid, eventually raising its offer to 650 million pounds before the British government stepped in to consider the offers in March.

The government asked the Monopolies and Mergers' Commission to investigate the bids, deciding in July that both could go ahead on condition that a number of Lloyds' wholesale operations were sold off.

Gehe is now set to become a major player in British retail pharmacy. Lloyds' 900-plus pharmacies will be added to around 360 owned by Gehe's existing British chain AAH, which means that it will overtake current market leader Boots Co Plc's 1,200 outlets on a store-count basis.
Unichem's own chain of Moss chemists will remain well behind with around 470 outlets.

Analysts said both companies had hoped that the addition of the Lloyds chain would bring major benefits on supply, purchasing and advertising. Gehe steps up its presence at a time of increasing competition from Britain's powerful supermarket businesses and pressure from the government to end the fixed-price regime for over-the-counter drugs.
